Human immunodeficiency virus is tied to immunodeficiency-associated Burkitt lymphoma and is a general lymphoma risk. Tell: the splenic marginal zone association is hepatitis C.
Human herpesvirus 8 is on the list of chronic infections that raise non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk, without a link to the splenic subtype. Tell: spleen plus marginal zone means hepatitis C.

set1.q: What are Reed-Sternberg cells?
opts: Correct. Hodgkin lymphoma is a type of B-cell lymphoma characterized by few malignant cells, the Reed-Sternberg cells, which are binucleated, neoplastic B cells, set among numerous immune effector cells.
Benign macrophages clearing dying lymphoma cells give the starry sky appearance of Burkitt lymphoma. Tell: macrophages are the Burkitt stars; Reed-Sternberg cells are the malignant cells of Hodgkin.
Plasma cells, terminally differentiated B cells, give rise to the plasma cell disorders such as multiple myeloma. Tell: Reed-Sternberg cells are binucleated B cells, not plasma cells.

set1.q: At what size is a persistent, enlarging lymph node considered significant enough for biopsy?
opts: Half a centimeter is well under the threshold; biopsy is reserved for significant enlargement of 2 cm. Tell: the cut-off is 2 cm.
One centimeter is below the stated threshold of 2 cm for significant enlargement. Tell: double it.
Correct. Excisional biopsy is reserved for significant enlargement (2 cm), persistent, and progressively increasing in size. The whole node is removed so its architecture can be seen.
Five centimeters overshoots; a persistent, progressively enlarging node of 2 cm already qualifies. Tell: waiting for 5 cm would delay diagnosis.

opts: Correct. MGUS (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance) carries a risk of myeloma progression of about 1% per year. Smoldering myeloma progresses faster, about 10% per year.
About 10% per year is the progression rate of smoldering myeloma. Tell: smoldering is 10%; the earlier, lower-risk state is about 1%.
A quarter per year overstates it; the premalignant state carries about 1% per year. Tell: low risk of progression.

set1.q: How is early, non-bulky stage I or II Hodgkin lymphoma without B symptoms treated?
opts: Watch and wait is not the plan for Hodgkin lymphoma; early, non-bulky stage I or II disease is treated with a short course of chemotherapy. Tell: early Hodgkin is treated, briefly.
Allogeneic stem cell transplant may be required after relapse following first-line therapy. Tell: transplant is for relapse, not early disease.

Correct. Early stage I and stage II Hodgkin lymphoma without bulk or B symptoms is treated with a short course of chemotherapy, historically ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine). Bulky disease or B symptoms add radiation.
Chemotherapy plus radiation is for bulky stage I or II disease or B symptoms. Tell: early, non-bulky disease without B symptoms needs chemotherapy alone, short course.

set1.q: How much is Hodgkin lymphoma risk raised in a same-sex sibling of a patient?
opts: Twice is the male excess in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, not the Hodgkin sibling risk. Tell: Hodgkin sibling risk is tenfold.
Four times understates the sibling risk, which is 10 times. Tell: the same-sex sibling figure is ten.
Correct. Same-sex siblings of a patient have a 10 times increased risk of also developing Hodgkin lymphoma. Epstein-Barr virus is a suspected risk factor, found in 40-50% of cases.
Fifty times overstates it; the increase for a same-sex sibling is 10 times. Tell: a tenfold rise.

set1.q: How is asymptomatic chronic lymphocytic leukemia without rapid progression managed?
opts: Targeted therapy is started for symptomatic disease or rapid progression, not for a stable asymptomatic patient. Tell: no symptoms and no rapid doubling means observe.

Allogeneic stem cell transplant may be required for Hodgkin lymphoma that relapses after first-line treatment, not for asymptomatic chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: stable, symptom-free disease is watched.
Radiation is the treatment for a single-node, non-aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: an asymptomatic leukemia needs no treatment until symptoms or rapid progression appear.

Correct. Asymptomatic patients may be observed, watch and wait, until there is evidence of rapid progression (a lymphocyte count doubling in under 6 months) or disease-related symptoms. Treatment begins with symptomatic disease or rapid progression.

opts: Admission is needed to start therapy
Hospital admission is described for aggressive lymphomas with electrolyte abnormalities, not for this leukemia. Tell: chronic lymphocytic leukemia care is outpatient pills or infusions.
No follow-up is needed once stable
Patients will require follow-ups for lab monitoring and treatment. Tell: monitoring continues even when the outlook is good.
The long-term prognosis is likely very good, with 5-year relative survival about 88%. Tell: poor outcomes belong to Richter transformation, not to the usual course.

set1.q: Under the R-ISS (Revised International Staging System), a myeloma patient who meets neither stage I nor stage III criteria is which stage?
opts: Stage I requires every favorable criterion: beta-2 microglobulin under 3.5 mg/L, albumin at least 3.5 g/dL, standard-risk chromosomes and normal lactate dehydrogenase. Tell: missing stage I makes it II or III.

Correct. In the R-ISS (Revised International Staging System), stage II is defined as not stage I or III. Stage I needs low beta-2 microglobulin, normal albumin, standard-risk chromosomes and normal lactate dehydrogenase; stage III needs high beta-2 microglobulin with high-risk chromosomes and high lactate dehydrogenase.
Stage III requires beta-2 microglobulin of 5.5 mg/L or more with high-risk chromosomes and high lactate dehydrogenase. Tell: not meeting stage III leaves stage II.
The R-ISS (Revised International Staging System) has only three stages. Tell: the stages are I, II and III.

set1.q: What is the main focus of treatment in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma?
opts: Rituximab targets cluster of differentiation 20 on B cells; T cells do not express it, so T-cell lymphoma regimens omit it. Tell: no rituximab for T-cell disease.

Correct. Treatments for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides) focus on the cutaneous manifestations, because there is often no visceral involvement. The aggressive Sezary form brings severe itching that lowers quality of life.
Visceral involvement is often absent in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, so it is not the main target. Tell: the skin is the disease.
The lesions resemble fungal infections but are lymphoma, so antifungals do not treat them. Tell: fungal-looking skin lesions here are T-cell lymphoma.

Correct. Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma is very aggressive, associated with human T-lymphotropic virus 1, and more common in the Caribbean, Central America and South America.
Anaplastic large cell lymphoma is an aggressive T-cell lymphoma but carries no viral link on the list. Tell: the virus-linked type is adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.

About 88% is the 5-year relative survival of chronic lymphocytic leukemia since 2013. Tell: myeloma survival is lower, about 60%.

Fifteen percent is the T-cell or natural killer-cell share, not the B-cell share. Tell: B-cell lymphomas are the large majority.
The split is not even; B-cell types make up about 85%. Tell: the T-cell and natural killer-cell types are the minority at 15%.

opts: Myeloma is by definition symptomatic; it is smoldering myeloma, a more indolent process, that is often monitored. Tell: active myeloma is treated.
Eradication is not the stated aim; the disease remains incurable and relapsing. Tell: prolong remission, protect quality of life.
Long remissions and quality of life
Correct. Because myeloma is by definition symptomatic and considered incurable, the goal of treatment is maintaining prolonged remissions to improve survival while maintaining quality of life.

set1.q: Which regimen is an example of multi-drug therapy for aggressive B-cell lymphoma?
opts: CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) without rituximab

CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) without rituximab is the similar regimen used for T-cell lymphomas, because T cells have no cluster of differentiation 20; it leaves out the rituximab of the B-cell example. Tell: a B-cell lymphoma keeps the rituximab.
Venetoclax plus obinutuzumab for a fixed duration

Venetoclax, a B-cell lymphoma 2 inhibitor, combined with a monoclonal antibody such as obinutuzumab for a fixed duration is a chronic lymphocytic leukemia targeted therapy. Tell: that is a leukemia combination; aggressive lymphoma gets rituximab with CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone).
Rituximab plus CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone)

Correct. Aggressive B-cell lymphomas are often treated with multi-drug chemotherapy such as R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, prednisone). Rituximab is the anti-cluster of differentiation 20 monoclonal antibody.
ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) without rituximab

ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) was historically the short course of chemotherapy for early-stage Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: that regimen is Hodgkin; rituximab with CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) is aggressive B-cell.

set1.q: How is chronic lymphocytic leukemia most often first discovered?
opts: A very rapidly growing swelling, with changes visible during the course of one day, describes Burkitt lymphoma, a very aggressive lymphoma. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia nodes are painless, firm and mobile, and the disease is often silent. Tell: rapid growth means Burkitt.

Correct. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is frequently diagnosed while the patient is asymptomatic, on routine blood work that shows a lymphocytosis. Symptoms, when present, come from nodes, cytopenias or B symptoms.
Only 5-10% of patients develop B symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fevers), so they are not the usual route to diagnosis. Tell: most patients have no symptoms at all when the count is found.
Thrombocytopenia can cause easy bruising and bleeding, but most patients are asymptomatic when diagnosed. Tell: bleeding is a cytopenia symptom, not the common first clue.

opts: Correct. The work-up includes LDH (lactate dehydrogenase), which reflects rapid proliferation, alongside a complete blood count for cytopenias from marrow involvement and chemistries to rule out tumor lysis syndrome.
Bone marrow involvement shows as cytopenias on the complete blood count. Tell: cytopenias reflect the marrow; lactate dehydrogenase reflects rapid proliferation.
Hyperviscosity comes from excess immunoglobulin M in lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, not from lactate dehydrogenase. Tell: the enzyme marks fast cell turnover.
A monoclonal protein on serum protein electrophoresis is characteristic of multiple myeloma. Tell: lactate dehydrogenase tracks proliferation, not a paraprotein.

Multi-drug chemotherapy is the approach to aggressive B-cell lymphomas. Tell: one node and non-aggressive means radiation.
Autologous transplant improves survival in transplant-eligible multiple myeloma. Tell: transplant belongs to myeloma; a single indolent node gets radiation.

opts: The Caribbean, Central America and South America are where adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, linked to human T-lymphotropic virus 1, is more common. Tell: Caribbean origin points to that T-cell lymphoma, not to chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

African Americans carry a higher risk of multiple myeloma than other races. The group named for chronic lymphocytic leukemia is Eastern European and Jewish descent. Tell: African American race is a stated risk for multiple myeloma.
Sub-Saharan Africa and New Guinea are where endemic Burkitt lymphoma, strongly tied to Epstein-Barr virus, is seen. Tell: sub-Saharan Africa means endemic Burkitt, not chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
Correct. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is more common in Eastern Europeans and in people of Jewish descent, and twice as common in males. No occupational or environmental risk factor is known.

set1.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: Excisional lymph node biopsy is how a lymphoma is diagnosed, because the node architecture must be seen. This leukemia is confirmed from the blood. Tell: node biopsy is for lymphoma; flow cytometry is for this leukemia.

Serum protein electrophoresis shows the monoclonal protein of multiple myeloma and the other plasma cell disorders. Tell: a monoclonal protein means a plasma cell disorder; a clonal B-cell population on flow means chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

Correct. The diagnosis is confirmed by flow cytometry, which identifies the clonal B-cell population, coexpressing the cluster of differentiation markers 19 and 5. A bone marrow biopsy is usually not required.
A bone marrow biopsy is usually not required to diagnose chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: the blood itself is examined by flow cytometry to show the clone.

The Revised International Staging System stages multiple myeloma with beta-2 microglobulin, albumin, chromosomes and lactate dehydrogenase. Tell: that is myeloma staging.

Allopurinol, a hypouricemic agent, is taken, not stopped, when treatment starts, along with plenty of fluids. Tell: take it when treatment starts.

Correct. Upon starting treatment, patients should drink plenty of fluids and take allopurinol (a hypouricemic agent), given in advance because tumor lysis syndrome should be anticipated. Care is managed by a hematologist, ideally a lymphoma expert.
Limit fluids to protect the heart

Fluid restriction works against the plan: tumor lysis syndrome can cause acute renal failure from uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals and requires aggressive fluid hydration. Tell: the instruction is to drink plenty of fluids.

Stage II needs organomegaly, hepatomegaly and/or splenomegaly, on top of lymphocytosis and lymphadenopathy. Tell: no enlarged liver or spleen means stage I.

No surgical step is described; treatment is prompt multi-agent chemotherapy after emergent hematology referral. Tell: transfer to hematology, not surgery.
Watch and wait suits indolent disease such as follicular lymphoma, not a lymphoma that can double within a day. Tell: Burkitt never waits.

Stage 2 is two or more node regions on the same side of the diaphragm. Tell: crossing the diaphragm moves it to stage 3.

opts: A lactate dehydrogenase above the upper limit of normal is a stage III criterion. Tell: stage I needs a normal lactate dehydrogenase.

Beta-2 microglobulin of 5.5 mg/L or more
Beta-2 microglobulin of 5.5 mg/L or more, regardless of albumin, is a stage III criterion. Tell: high beta-2 microglobulin points to stage III.

set2.q: What is the usual management of follicular lymphoma that causes no symptoms?
opts: Correct. Follicular lymphoma frequently needs no treatment (watch and wait), though it may be treated with intermittent low-intensity therapy if symptomatic; high-risk disease may need more aggressive therapy. It is incurable, but often needs no treatment or only intermittent treatment.
Multi-agent chemotherapy is the approach to aggressive B-cell lymphomas. Tell: an asymptomatic indolent lymphoma is watched; intensive therapy is kept for high-risk disease.
Rapid transfer of care is required for Burkitt lymphoma, whose doubling time is extremely fast. Tell: emergency transfer is for Burkitt, not an indolent lymphoma.
Allogeneic stem cell transplant may be required for Hodgkin lymphoma that relapses after first-line treatment. Tell: asymptomatic follicular lymphoma is observed.

set2.q: How is venetoclax typically given in chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: Maintenance therapy after autologous transplant has been shown to improve overall survival in multiple myeloma. Tell: transplant maintenance belongs to myeloma; venetoclax is a time-limited combination here.
With an antibody, for a fixed time

Correct. Venetoclax, the B-cell lymphoma 2 inhibitor, is combined with monoclonal antibodies for a fixed duration. That contrasts with Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors, which are usually continuous when used alone.
Continuous monotherapy describes the Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as ibrutinib. Tell: venetoclax is paired with an antibody and given for a set time.
Radiation is used for a single-node, non-aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma, not combined with venetoclax. Tell: venetoclax pairs with a monoclonal antibody.

set2.q: In chronic lymphocytic leukemia, rapid progression that ends watchful waiting is a lymphocyte count doubling within what time?
opts: Two months is stricter than the definition; doubling in under 6 months already counts as rapid progression. Tell: the window is 6 months.

Three months is how long an absolute lymphocyte count above 5,000 must last for the diagnostic blood criterion, not the doubling time. Tell: 3 months diagnoses; doubling in under 6 months triggers treatment.

Correct. Observation continues until rapid progression, defined as the lymphocyte count doubling in under 6 months, or until disease-related symptoms appear. Either one is the indication to start treatment.
Twelve months is too loose; rapid progression is a doubling within 6 months. Tell: the cut-off is half that, 6 months.

set2.q: How does Hodgkin lymphoma typically spread?
opts: Osteolytic, punched-out bone lesions are a feature of multiple myeloma. Tell: Hodgkin spreads through contiguous nodes.

Correct. Hodgkin lymphoma is marked by contiguous spread through the lymph nodes in an orderly fashion. Its malignant cells are few binucleated Reed-Sternberg cells among numerous immune effector cells.
Hodgkin lymphoma spreads contiguously in an orderly fashion, not by skipping. Tell: orderly is the key word.
Skin lesions that resemble fungal infections are the presentation of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Tell: Hodgkin spreads node to adjacent node.

set2.q: In tumor lysis syndrome, which released product carries the largest risk of death?
opts: Uric acid precipitates in the renal tubules and causes acute renal failure, which allopurinol helps prevent. Tell: uric acid harms the kidney; potassium causes the fatal arrhythmia.
Calcium phosphate crystals form in the tubules, but calcium itself is not the released product named as the largest risk. Tell: hyperkalemia drives the arrhythmia.

Correct. Tumor lysis syndrome releases potassium, phosphorus and uric acid; the largest risk is hyperkalemia, which leads to arrhythmia and potential death. It is a medical emergency needing aggressive intravenous fluids.

set2.q: Which non-Hodgkin lymphoma is classed as indolent?

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is listed among the very aggressive lymphomas, not with follicular, marginal zone and small lymphocytic disease. Tell: diffuse large B-cell is aggressive; follicular is indolent.
T-cell leukemia/lymphoma is listed at the very aggressive end of the range, alongside Burkitt and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Tell: it is among the very aggressive types.

Correct. Non-Hodgkin lymphomas range from very aggressive (Burkitt, diffuse large B-cell, T-cell leukemia/lymphoma) to indolent (follicular, marginal zone, small lymphocytic). Follicular lymphoma is the most common indolent histology.

Adults in their 20s form one incidence peak, but inferior results are tied to older age. Tell: young age is not the adverse factor.
Bulky disease, not non-bulky early disease, gives inferior results. Tell: small, early disease does well.
Cervical nodes are the usual presentation and carry no stated adverse meaning. Tell: the adverse groups are older age, bulk and certain subtypes.

Helicobacter pylori gastritis is tied to gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma in two thirds of cases, not to a reactive lymphocytosis. Tell: H. pylori means gastric lymphoma.

Hepatitis C is associated with splenic marginal zone lymphoma and is listed among the chronic infections that are non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk factors, not the named cause of atypical lymphocytosis. Tell: the mimic named is pertussis.
Lyme disease is listed among the chronic infections that raise non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk. Tell: a reactive lymphocytosis mimic here is pertussis.

set2.q: In the Rai classification, lymphocytosis with anemia, lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, and normal platelets, is which stage?
opts: Stage I is lymphocytosis with lymphadenopathy only. Tell: anemia moves the stage well past I.
Stage II is lymphocytosis, nodes and organomegaly without a cytopenia. Tell: the anemia takes this patient to stage III even with nodes and spleen present.
Correct. Rai stage III is lymphocytosis and anemia, with or without lymphadenopathy and/or organomegaly. Anemia outranks the nodes and spleen, and with normal platelets the stage does not reach IV.
Stage IV is defined by thrombocytopenia, with or without anemia. Tell: platelets are normal, so the anemia sets the stage at III.

No role for ultrasound is described in the myeloma work-up. Tell: bone lesions are imaged with whole-body computed tomography.
Imaging of the brain is not part of the myeloma bone work-up. Tell: the whole skeleton is imaged with computed tomography.

set2.q: Which organ enlargement is most often found on exam in chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: A nasal-region mass points to extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, not chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: this leukemia enlarges the spleen in about 40%.

set2.q: Outside of lymphoma, in which setting can tumor lysis syndrome also be seen?

Correct. Tumor lysis syndrome can be seen outside lymphomas, in acute lymphocytic leukemia and acute myelogenous leukemia with marked leukocytosis. Within lymphoma it can occur spontaneously in highly aggressive types such as Burkitt.

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance is an asymptomatic plasma cell condition with a low risk of progression, not a rapidly breaking-down tumor. Tell: tumor lysis needs rapid tumor breakdown.

Follicular lymphoma is indolent and frequently needs no treatment (watch and wait), so there is no rapid tumor breakdown. Tell: tumor lysis follows rapid breakdown, as in aggressive lymphomas or leukemia with a high count.

Active multiple myeloma with end-organ damage

opts: This reverses the groups: children do best, above 90%, and adults reach 50-90%. Tell: the pediatric figure is the higher one.

Burkitt lymphoma is very aggressive, but with early multi-agent chemotherapy its long-term prognosis is excellent. Tell: aggressive does not mean hopeless here.

Novel therapies, including cellular therapies and bispecific antibodies, are currently used for relapsed myeloma. Tell: they are kept for relapse, not first-line.
Proteasome inhibitor, immunomodulatory drug and steroid

Correct. Newly diagnosed patients are treated with a 3- or 4-drug regimen built on a proteasome inhibitor and immunomodulatory drug backbone with steroids. Transplant candidates add autologous transplant and maintenance.
Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor given continuously

Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors, usually continuous as monotherapy, are a chronic lymphocytic leukemia targeted therapy. Tell: myeloma starts on proteasome inhibitor, immunomodulatory drug and steroid.
Rituximab with multi-drug chemotherapy is the aggressive B-cell lymphoma regimen. Tell: plasma cell disease uses a proteasome inhibitor backbone.

set2.q: At what rate does monoclonal B lymphocytosis progress to chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: Correct. Monoclonal B lymphocytosis, a count below 5,000 with no nodes, organomegaly, cytopenias or symptoms, progresses to chronic lymphocytic leukemia at a rate of 1-2% per year.
About 10% per year is the progression rate of smoldering myeloma to multiple myeloma. Tell: 10% belongs to smoldering myeloma; 1-2% to monoclonal B lymphocytosis.
A quarter per year overstates the risk; monoclonal B lymphocytosis progresses at only 1-2% per year. Tell: it is a low-risk precursor.
Above 50% within 2 years is the risk in some high-risk smoldering myeloma groups, not the yearly rate for monoclonal B lymphocytosis. Tell: 1-2% per year here.

set2.q: Which T-cell lymphoma often affects the nasal region?
opts: Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma is named for the liver and spleen, not the nose. Tell: the nasal one is extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma.
Intestinal T-cell lymphomas involve the bowel. Tell: a nasal mass points to the extranodal natural killer/T-cell type.

Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified, is the most common T-cell lymphoma (one third of cases) but is not tied to the nose. Tell: most common is peripheral; nasal is extranodal natural killer/T-cell.

Correct. Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma often affects the nasal region. It is one of the diverse T-cell lymphomas, alongside peripheral T-cell (most common), anaplastic large cell and hepatosplenic types.

set2.q: Which statement describes the prognosis of indolent lymphomas?
opts: Curable in about half with chemotherapy
Cure with chemotherapy describes aggressive lymphomas, not indolent ones, which stay incurable even with treatment. Tell: aggressive lymphomas can be cured; indolent ones are incurable but slow.
More than 90% alive at 5 years describes Hodgkin lymphoma, which is generally curable. Tell: that is Hodgkin, not an indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Survival under 2 years is not the outlook for indolent lymphomas; patients often survive 10-15 or more years. Tell: indolent means incurable but slow.

Correct. Indolent lymphomas are incurable but survival is often 10-15 or more years with intermittent treatment, with a risk of progression to an aggressive, difficult-to-treat lymphoma. Aggressive lymphomas, by contrast, are often treatable.

set2.q: Which set of findings defines MGUS (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance)?
opts: M-protein under 3 g/dL, plasma cells under 10%

Correct. MGUS (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance) is by definition asymptomatic: M-protein below 3 g/dL, clonal bone marrow plasma cells below 10% and no myeloma-defining characteristics. It progresses to myeloma at about 1% per year.

An M-protein above 3 g/dL with 10-60% marrow plasma cells and no myeloma-defining events is smoldering myeloma. Tell: higher numbers without CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) features mean smoldering.
Plasma cells 10% or more with bone lesions
Plasma cells of 10% or more plus a CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) feature such as bone lesions defines multiple myeloma. Tell: an end-organ feature means myeloma.
A lymphocyte count below 5,000 with no nodes, organomegaly or cytopenias is monoclonal B lymphocytosis. Tell: that is a lymphocyte clone, not a plasma cell clone.

set2.q: Where is the lymphadenopathy of Hodgkin lymphoma usually found?
opts: Correct. Hodgkin lymphoma is characterized by painless asymptomatic lymphadenopathy (70%), usually cervical, but it could be supraclavicular or mediastinal. A mediastinal mass may show on chest X-ray.
The usual site named is cervical, with supraclavicular or mediastinal as alternatives. Tell: think neck first.
Axillary nodes are not the usual site; the typical Hodgkin node is cervical. Tell: the neck is the classic location.
Abdominal nodes are not named; Hodgkin lymphoma is usually cervical, supraclavicular or mediastinal. Tell: above the diaphragm, in the neck.

set2.q: How is tumor lysis syndrome prevented before treating an aggressive lymphoma?
opts: Tumor lysis syndrome requires aggressive intravenous fluid hydration; restricting fluids would worsen crystal precipitation. Tell: give fluids, never restrict them.

Correct. Tumor lysis syndrome should be anticipated in aggressive lymphoma, and patients are given allopurinol (a hypouricemic agent) and fluids in advance. Patients are told to drink plenty of fluids and take allopurinol on starting treatment.
Tumor lysis releases potassium, and hyperkalemia is its greatest danger, so extra potassium is the opposite of prevention. Tell: the goal is clearing products, not adding potassium.
Aggressive lymphomas, especially Burkitt, need prompt treatment; prevention means preparing with fluids and allopurinol, not waiting. Tell: anticipate and protect, then treat.

set2.q: What causes the renal dysfunction of multiple myeloma?
opts: Correct. Renal dysfunction in myeloma often comes from light chain and calcium phosphate deposition. Anemia is multifactorial, from renal dysfunction and bone marrow involvement.
Uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals in the tubules cause the renal failure of tumor lysis syndrome. Tell: uric acid is tumor lysis; light chains are myeloma.
Hyperviscosity is not the named cause of myeloma kidney injury, which is light chain and calcium phosphate deposition. Tell: myeloma kidneys clog with light chains.

Osteoclast activation releases calcium into the bloodstream; the kidney injury itself is named as light chain and calcium phosphate deposition. Tell: osteoclasts raise calcium; the main kidney injury named is light chain deposition.

set2.q: Which group is at higher risk of developing multiple myeloma?
opts: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is more common in Eastern Europeans and those of Jewish descent. Tell: myeloma's race risk is African American.
Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma is more common in the Caribbean, Central and South America. Tell: myeloma's higher-risk group is African American.
Endemic Burkitt lymphoma is seen largely in sub-Saharan Africa and New Guinea. Tell: myeloma's race risk is African American.

Correct. African Americans are at higher risk of developing multiple myeloma than other races. Other risks are older age (most diagnoses over 65), family history, prior monoclonal gammopathy or smoldering myeloma, and radiation, chemical or occupational exposures.

set2.q: What is the median age at diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: Forty is far too young for the median; chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a disease of older adults with a median age of 70 years. Tell: think of an older adult found on routine blood work, not a young adult.
Fifty-five falls well short of the median age of 70 years for chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: the median sits a decade above 60, not below it.

Correct. The median age at diagnosis, and at onset, of chronic lymphocytic leukemia is 70 years, so it is a disease of older adults. That elderly onset is one reason many patients are expected to die with the disease rather than from it.
Eighty-five overshoots; the median age at diagnosis is 70 years. Tell: the median is 70, so half of patients are diagnosed younger than that.

set2.q: About what share of non-Hodgkin lymphoma patients develop extranodal disease?
opts: Ten percent understates it; about half develop extranodal disease. Tell: extranodal spread is common, not rare.
A quarter understates it; about half of patients develop lymphoma outside the nodes. Tell: think one in two.

Correct. Approximately half of patients develop extranodal disease, lymphoma outside the lymph nodes, such as central nervous system lymphoma. Peripheral lymphadenopathy is present in more than two thirds.

set2.q: Which agent used in chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor?
opts: Venetoclax is the B-cell lymphoma 2 inhibitor, combined with monoclonal antibodies for a fixed duration. Tell: the kinase inhibitors end in -brutinib.
Obinutuzumab is a monoclonal antibody, listed with rituximab and ofatumumab. Tell: monoclonal antibodies end in -mab; the kinase inhibitors end in -brutinib.

Allopurinol is a hypouricemic agent given with fluids in advance in aggressive lymphoma, where tumor lysis syndrome should be anticipated. Tell: it is supportive care, not a targeted leukemia therapy.
